mcqs.question: A cache node's data set has outgrown its available memory and its request rate has plateaued near the node's throughput ceiling. What's the correct fix?
options: Reduce the TTL on all keys so the cache holds less data
Switch from LRU to FIFO eviction to free up more capacity
Add more cache nodes and shard the data and load across them
Move the cache in front of a CDN instead of the application
mcqs.explanation: Once a single node is genuinely out of both memory and throughput headroom, the fix is horizontal — more nodes sharing the data and load, the same logic as scaling a stateless tier. Shortening TTLs or switching eviction policy might buy a little room but doesn't address a real capacity ceiling, and a CDN solves a different problem (edge delivery, not internal cache capacity).

mcqs.question: Why does `hash(key) % number_of_nodes` sharding cause trouble when a node is added or removed?
options: It has no trouble at all — this is the standard sharding approach used in production
It makes the cache cluster slower on every single lookup
It only works with string keys, not numeric ones
Almost every key's assigned node changes at once, effectively invalidating nearly the whole cache
mcqs.explanation: Because the modulus itself changes, the vast majority of keys land on a different node than before, turning a routine node change into a near-total cache invalidation — this is exactly why consistent hashing exists as an alternative. It doesn't slow down individual lookups, and it works fine with numeric keys too; the problem is specifically about node-count changes.

mcqs.question: A single very hot cache key expires, and thousands of concurrent requests all miss on it within the same millisecond. What is this scenario called, and why is it dangerous?
options: A cache stampede — all the requests independently hit the database at once, potentially overwhelming it
Cache poisoning — the cache is storing incorrect data
A cache stampede — but it's harmless since the cache is designed to handle misses
This is expected steady-state behavior and requires no mitigation
mcqs.explanation: This is the classic cache stampede: many simultaneous misses on the same key all fall through to the database at once, and for a truly hot key that can be enough load to take the database down. It's not cache poisoning (that's about wrong data being cached), it isn't harmless just because misses are a normal event, and it does warrant mitigation.

mcqs.question: A team has many small, independent client services and doesn't want each one to reimplement and stay in sync on cache-routing logic. Which architecture fits better?
options: Client-side sharding, so each client controls its own routing
Proxy-based clustering, so the routing logic lives in one place all clients share
No sharding — a single cache node is simpler for many clients
Client-side sharding, but only for the largest client service
mcqs.explanation: A proxy centralizes the hashing/routing logic so clients stay simple and don't need to agree on or duplicate it — exactly what fits many independent, heterogeneous clients. Client-side sharding pushes that complexity into every client instead, which is the opposite of what's wanted here, and a single node reintroduces the original capacity problem this topic is solving.

mcqs.question: A team deploys a brand-new, completely empty cache cluster and immediately routes full production traffic to it. What's the likely outcome?
options: The cache gracefully warms up with no impact, since misses are handled the same as hits
The full request load hits the database directly, since every request is a miss on an empty cache
The cluster automatically pre-loads itself from the database before accepting traffic
Nothing changes, since cache warm-up doesn't affect database load
mcqs.explanation: An empty cache means every request misses, so the database receives the entire production load at once — precisely the load the cache exists to absorb. There's no automatic pre-load or graceful warm-up unless it's explicitly engineered (pre-populating keys or a staged rollout), and database load is very much affected.
